title: AWS Network Firewall
explanation:
AWS Network Firewall is a managed, stateful network firewall and intrusion prevention service (IPS) for VPCs. It provides fine-grained control over network traffic with deep packet inspection capabilities, going far beyond what security groups and NACLs can offer.

Network Firewall operates in a dedicated **firewall subnet** and inspects traffic as it passes through. Traffic is routed to the firewall using VPC route tables (typically via a Gateway Load Balancer endpoint that AWS manages internally). The firewall evaluates traffic against rule groups and takes actions (allow, drop, alert).

Rule types:
- **Stateless rules**: Evaluated first, process each packet independently (like NACLs). Can pass, drop, or forward to stateful rules
- **Stateful rules**: Track connection state and support deep packet inspection. Three formats:
  - 5-tuple rules: Source/dest IP, port, protocol with action
  - Domain list rules: Allow/deny traffic to specific domain names (e.g., block all except *.amazonaws.com)
  - Suricata-compatible IPS rules: Full intrusion detection/prevention using the open-source Suricata rule language

Deployment architecture:
- Firewall is deployed in a dedicated subnet (one per AZ)
- Internet-bound traffic is routed: Instance → Firewall subnet → NAT Gateway → IGW
- Ingress traffic: IGW → Firewall subnet → Application subnet
- Uses Gateway route tables on the IGW to intercept incoming traffic

For the SAP-C02 exam, Network Firewall questions test centralized inspection architectures (with Transit Gateway), domain-based filtering for egress control, IPS/IDS requirements, and integration with AWS Firewall Manager for multi-account governance.
analogy: Network Firewall is like an advanced airport security checkpoint with X-ray machines and behavioral analysis. Security groups are the boarding pass check (basic allow/deny at the gate), NACLs are the terminal entrance check (checks everyone entering/leaving). But Network Firewall is the full security screening — it opens your bags (deep packet inspection), checks for prohibited items (IPS signatures), and can even read the labels on your packages (domain filtering) to decide if you can proceed.
keyPoints: Managed stateful firewall with deep packet inspection, IPS/IDS, and domain-based filtering — far beyond security groups and NACLs
Supports Suricata-compatible IPS rules for detecting and blocking known attack signatures and CVE exploits
Domain list rules enable egress filtering — allow traffic only to approved domains (e.g., *.amazonaws.com) and block everything else
Deployed in a dedicated firewall subnet with traffic routed through it via VPC route tables and gateway route tables
Integrates with AWS Firewall Manager for centralized rule management across multiple accounts in an AWS Organization
Stateless rules are evaluated first (fast path for known-good/known-bad traffic), then remaining traffic passes to the stateful engine
Logs can be sent to S3, CloudWatch Logs, or Kinesis Data Firehose for analysis and alerting

examKeywords.definition: A managed stateful network firewall and IPS for VPCs supporting deep packet inspection, domain filtering, and Suricata-compatible intrusion prevention rules.
An open-source IPS rule format supported by AWS Network Firewall for detecting and blocking network-based attacks using signature matching.
A Network Firewall capability that allows or denies traffic based on the destination domain name (SNI/Host header), enabling egress control without IP-based rules.
AWS service for centrally managing firewall rules (Network Firewall, WAF, security groups) across multiple accounts in an AWS Organization.

commonMistakes: Deploying Network Firewall without a dedicated firewall subnet — it must be in its own subnet with specific routing to intercept traffic
Confusing Network Firewall (Layer 3-7 deep packet inspection, IPS, domain filtering) with security groups (Layer 4 allow-only rules) or NACLs (Layer 4 stateless rules)
Not configuring gateway route tables on the IGW — without them, inbound traffic bypasses the firewall entirely
Using Network Firewall for simple port-based filtering that security groups can handle — it adds cost and latency for basic use cases
Forgetting to enable logging — without logs, you cannot detect blocked threats or troubleshoot connectivity issues caused by firewall rules
